comments.text: Actually the Battle of the Aleutian Islands represents a turning point of the War about as significant as Midway. comments.author: @obliograce3551
comments.text: ✅ Just to mention it, the Aleutian Islands did play an inadvertent but a significant role in WW2. Yes, the Aleutian Islands did play a role in faking out the Japanese to keep aircraft carriers away from Midway. But, after the ensuing battle at Dutch Harbor, on July 10, 1942, a flipped-over Zero was found after a bad landing, still largely intact on Akutan Island in Alaska’s Aleutian Islands. The Japanese Zero had been doing a lot of damage against Allied forces in the Pacific. This fully functional captured Zero allowed the allied forces to take it a part, and test fly it to learn all about its strengths and its weaknesses. And that as much as anything made allied forces understand how to defeat the Zero.

replies.text:
While, there is evidence that the Polynesians intermixed with pre-Columbian indigenous South Americans around 1,000 years ago, there is no evidence that I'm aware of* that the Incas came entirely from people who sailed across the Pacific 

Also, the Incas didn't cross the Bering Landbridge — they descended from pre-historic peoples who crossed-over from Siberia into Western North America a couple tens of thousands of years ago. Those people migrated around North America over the next millennia, ultimately filtering into South America; and, one of the cultures that would arise from them was the Incas. This was a long process which spanned many thousands of years and didn't happen overnight (relatively-speaking)

(*: I am not a professional archeologist and/or anthropologist and/or geneticist — heck, I never even finished college; but, I do love watching scientific videos here on AdTube)
They took hang gliders

I believe the only evidence we rely on is based on the migration of the sweet potato from the Pacific to the Americas.

But yeah, Geoff has the migration history confused, there were multiple (at least 3) major migration groups over the last 20k+ years. Groups like the Inuit and Aztecs are not closely related by blood.
